newsitem.title: USA: FAA sets rules to limit air noise over Grand Canyon.
newsitem.headline: FAA sets rules to limit air noise over Grand Canyon.

text.p: Likening noise levels in parts of the Grand Canyon to Times Square on New Year's Eve, Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt on Tuesday announced steps to reduce the din from air tours over the canyon.
Under a new rule set by the Federal Aviation Administration, 80 percent of the air space over Grand Canyon National Park will be closed to commercial air tours, up from the current 40 percent.

The rule, which will take effect in May, sets dusk-to-dawn curfews for commercial sightseeing operations over the eastern end of the park. It also caps the number of commercial tour flights over the park at the 1996 level, estimated to be 80,000-90,000 flights.
The FAA also issued a proposed rule to phase out use of noisier aircraft in the park by 2008 by using technologies for quieter aircraft.

"The overflight noise at the Grand Canyon has been a continuing source of irritation and frustration. At peak periods of summer overflights, the south rim of the Grand Canyon is noisier than Time Square on New Year's Eve," Babbitt said at a news conference.

"The difference is the Grand Canyon is a national park, and American citizens should have the right to take their children there, and experience the grandeur...without the distraction of noise associated with living under the flight path of a municipal airport," he said.
But aircraft groups said the rule would compromise safety by pushing aircraft into a smaller space and would restrict people's access to the park.
Environmental groups on the other hand said the rule would not go far enough to restoring the "natural quiet" of the canyon called for in a law Congress passed in 1987.
A coalition of eight air tour companies said they will sue to block the rules.

"The new rules are excessive, unwarranted and unjustified and won't serve park visitors at all, but will substantially harm our businesses and restrict access to the park for thousands of visitors including the elderly and the physically challenged," Jim Petty, president of Air Vegas Airlines and head of the coalition, said in a statement.
The Helicopter Association International called on the National Transportation Safety Board to hold hearings on the plan, and urged Congress to block the rule.

The rule, announced the day before entrance fees for the Grand Canyon and several other major national parks are to double to $20 per car from $10, should serve as a blueprint to reduce noise levels in other parks, Babbitt said.

The rule stemmed from the 1987 National Parks Overflight Act, which included provisions to regulate air traffice over the canyon and called for "substantial restoration of the natural quiet and experience of the park."
President Clinton in April ordered the Transportation and Interior departments to implement a rule to reduce the noise by the end of the year.
